note.text: Opposition compares categorical claims with the same subject S and predicate P. A says all S are P; E says no S are P; I says some S are P; O says some S are not P. Some means at least one. Under the standard set-based meanings, A/O and E/I are contradictory even when S is empty. For the full classroom square here, explicitly assume S exists. Then A/E are contrary and I/O subcontrary. Do not silently change terms or assume existence from an all-claim alone.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to identify opposition relations without changing the subject, predicate or existence assumptions. Builds on: argument parts and Form Four categorical forms. Leads to: using the square to infer truth values.

sections.heading: Understand the pattern
sections.text: Opposition compares categorical claims with the same subject S and predicate P. A says all S are P; E says no S are P; I says some S are P; O says some S are not P. Some means at least one. Under the standard set-based meanings, A/O and E/I are contradictory even when S is empty. For the full classroom square here, explicitly assume S exists. Then A/E are contrary and I/O subcontrary. Do not silently change terms or assume existence from an all-claim alone.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original model: S means club members and P means badge holders in one fixed fictional club. If members exist and some hold badges while others do not, A and E are false while I and O are true. If no members exist, the standard set-based A and E are both true; I and O are false. This second case shows why the full square needs an existence assumption.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Write A/E/I/O in words, hold the terms fixed and state whether S is assumed nonempty. Distinguish cannot both be true from cannot both be false. The spine title is truncated; this draft teaches opposition as a mode of immediate inference, subject to teacher terminology review.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve scope, terms and assumptions.
example: Changing S into teachers leaves the same opposition pair. Correction: Changing the class changes the compared claims.
A and O may both be false under these meanings. Correction: O asserts exactly the counterexample that denies A.
A and E cannot both be true even if no S exist under the standard meanings. Correction: With empty S both universals are true in the stated set-based interpretation.
I and O cannot both be true. Correction: A mixed class supplies a witness for each.
